case_analysis.focal_point: Whether, in evaluating an Atkins intellectual-disability claim, courts may (and if so how they must) consider the cumulative evidentiary effect of multiple IQ test scores—most of which are above 70—when determining whether a defendant has shown significantly subaverage intellectual functioning that renders him categorically ineligible for execution.
case_analysis.legal_provision: Eighth Amendment (as applied through Atkins v. Virginia’s categorical bar on executing persons with intellectual disability), with related federal statutory context under the Federal Death Penalty Act’s parallel prohibition, 18 U.S.C. § 3596(c).
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Alabama argues that its evidentiary framework is constitutionally permissible and that the Eleventh Circuit misapplied this Court’s Atkins-line precedents by allowing an intellectual-disability claim to proceed despite multiple IQ scores (e.g., 75, 74, 72, 78, 74) that do not make it likely the defendant’s true IQ is 70 or below. The State emphasizes federalism/experimentation in implementing Atkins, contends that courts may consider the overall pattern (i.e., the cumulative picture) created by repeated testing rather than treating any single score as dispositive, and maintains that the decision below unduly constrains States’ ability to enforce capital sentences by effectively relaxing the required proof of significantly subaverage intellectual functioning.
case_analysis.respondent_position: Smith argues that Atkins and subsequent Supreme Court decisions require an intellectually-disability inquiry aligned with current clinical standards, including recognition of measurement error in IQ testing (e.g., standard error of measurement) and avoidance of rigid cutoffs or score-counting rules that can mask true intellectual disability. He contends that courts should not use multiple above-70 scores cumulatively to defeat an Atkins claim in a way that functionally reinstates a bright-line threshold, and that the proper analysis requires a holistic assessment of intellectual functioning (including confidence intervals and other evidence) along with adaptive functioning and onset before age 18.

John Roberts.reasoning: Justice Kagan and Justice Sotomayor rightly warn that a “mostly-above-70” aggregation can become a functional bright-line rule that evades Hall and Moore by short-circuiting the adaptive-functioning and onset inquiry; I agree that is the constitutional failure mode we must guard against. But their argument does not show that considering multiple scores (with SEM) is itself unconstitutional—Hall condemned a rule that made a number dispositive and foreclosed further consideration, not ordinary evidentiary weighing of the full testing record in a holistic Atkins framework. Justice Gorsuch’s stare decisis point reinforces that we must apply Hall/Moore as written, which in my view supports a narrow reversal: permit cumulative consideration, but prohibit treating a score pattern as conclusive when SEM-adjusted ranges encompass 70 and require proceeding to the remaining prongs. On that minimal, precedent-respecting ground, the Eleventh Circuit’s apparent constraint improperly converts Hall into a one-way, one-score presumption and unduly narrows the discretion Atkins (and Congress via § 3596(c)) left to implement the categorical bar.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor and Justice Kagan offer the strongest point: that a “mostly-above-70” aggregation can, in practice, become a functional cutoff that evades Hall and Moore by short-circuiting adaptive-functioning and onset evidence. But that concern identifies potential evidentiary misuse, not a constitutional rule derivable from the Eighth Amendment’s text or its original public meaning, and it risks converting Hall’s anti-bright-line principle into a defendant-favoring presumption untethered to anything in Atkins or § 3596(c). As Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Alito explain, Hall condemned making an IQ number dispositive and foreclosing further inquiry; it did not forbid a factfinder from weighing multiple scores (with SEM) alongside other evidence in ordinary adjudication. Because the Eleventh Circuit appears to have treated SEM-adjacent scores as effectively controlling—and to have constrained cumulative assessment in a way our precedents do not compel—I would reverse.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor and Justice Kagan press the strongest point: that “mostly-above-70” aggregation can become a proxy bright-line cutoff that effectively short-circuits adaptive-deficits and onset, recreating the rigidity Hall and Moore condemned. But that risk goes to misapplication, not to a constitutional rule that any SEM-adjacent low score triggers prong-one satisfaction or disables ordinary factfinding across the full IQ record; Hall’s vice was making an IQ number dispositive and foreclosing the remainder of the inquiry, not permitting a court to weigh multiple scores with SEM as evidence. Chief Justice Roberts’s narrower approach best fits stare decisis: reverse any framework that treats a score pattern as conclusive (on either side) and make clear that when SEM-adjusted ranges encompass 70, courts may not terminate the analysis without considering adaptive functioning and onset, while still allowing cumulative assessment as part of the holistic Atkins/§ 3596(c) determination. Justice Gorsuch’s “score-counting” concern is addressed by rejecting mechanistic aggregation as outcome-determinative, not by constitutionalizing a one-way evidentiary presumption untethered to Atkins’s implementation discretion.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: I agree with Chief Justice Roberts that Hall and Moore do not create a one-low-score rule and that multiple IQ scores (properly adjusted for SEM) may be weighed, but his proposed “narrow reversal” understates how Alabama’s “mostly-above-70” aggregation can become the very kind of dispositive gatekeeping Hall condemned when it functionally ends prong one and prevents genuine consideration of adaptive deficits and onset. Justice Alito’s federalism/discretion point does not answer the Eighth Amendment reliability problem our precedents recognize: discretion cannot be used to recreate, by score-counting, a cutoff that predictably increases the risk of executing someone within the Atkins-protected class. Justice Gorsuch’s focus on avoiding “nonclinical distortions” reinforces that the constitutional flaw is not admitting multiple scores, but treating their accumulation as outcome-determinative despite SEM and testing conditions, thereby short-circuiting the holistic inquiry Hall/Moore require. Because the Eleventh Circuit’s approach can be read as insisting that SEM-range overlap with 70 keeps the door open to the full Atkins analysis (not as mandating prong-one satisfaction), I would affirm rather than reverse.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: The Chief Justice’s proposed “narrow reversal” usefully clarifies that Hall and Moore do not create a one-low-score rule and that multiple IQ scores (with SEM) may be weighed, but it still underspecifies the constitutional stopping point and risks blessing the very failure mode he acknowledges—using a mostly-above-70 pattern as a proxy cutoff that functionally forecloses prongs two and three. Justice Alito and Justice Kavanaugh are right that Hall polices rigidity rather than outcomes, yet Hall’s core demand is not merely that SEM be recited; it is that SEM meaningfully prevents an IQ-number gate from being dispositive when the error range keeps 70 in play, requiring a holistic Atkins inquiry rather than score-counting. Justice Thomas’s federalism critique would require retreating from Hall/Moore’s clinically grounded constraint, and under stare decisis I cannot accept that; our task is to enforce those precedents in a workable way that does not let aggregation become a “final and conclusive” cutoff by another name. On this record, the Eleventh Circuit’s approach appears to allow exactly that short-circuiting, so I remain with the Respondent.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: The Chief Justice is right that Hall and Moore do not impose a one-low-score rule and that multiple IQ scores may be weighed; nothing in § 3596(c) demands a defendant-favoring presumption. But Justice Sotomayor persuasively identifies the constitutional failure mode: a “mostly-above-70” tally can become a nonclinical proxy cutoff that, in practice, treats score patterns as dispositive and thereby forecloses a meaningful adaptive-deficits and onset inquiry even when SEM-adjusted ranges keep 70 in play—precisely what Hall condemned. Justice Thomas’s federalism critique would require narrowing Hall/Moore beyond stare decisis and beyond what their holdings, as written, require of courts applying a categorical Eighth Amendment bar. On an originalist/textualist approach, the constitutional floor is reliability in identifying the exempt class; I cannot endorse a framework that predictably recreates a bright-line gatekeeping rule by accumulation rather than by a single number.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s and Justice Kagan’s strongest point—that “mostly-above-70” aggregation can become a functional cutoff that evades Hall and Moore—is a real constitutional failure mode, but it is best addressed by prohibiting dispositive gatekeeping, not by disabling ordinary weighing of the full IQ record. As Chief Justice Roberts frames it, Hall condemned rules that make an IQ number conclusive and foreclose the adaptive-deficits/onset inquiry; it did not constitutionalize a one-way presumption that any SEM-adjacent low score satisfies prong one regardless of the broader record. Justice Gorsuch’s § 3596(c) point reinforces, for me, that the statute contemplates a judicial determination on the evidence, so long as the method is clinically grounded (including SEM) and does not terminate the Atkins analysis by score-counting. On that institutionalist, precedent-respecting approach, the Eleventh Circuit’s apparent constraint goes too far by converting Hall’s anti-rigidity principle into a defendant-favoring evidentiary ratchet rather than a ban on rigid cutoffs.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Justice Kagan and Justice Sotomayor identify the real constitutional danger: a “mostly-above-70” aggregation can be deployed as a functional cutoff that renders SEM consideration illusory and effectively forecloses the adaptive-functioning and onset inquiry Hall and Moore require. But under a textualist and originalist approach constrained by stare decisis, Hall/Moore police rigidity and nonclinical distortions; they do not forbid a factfinder from weighing multiple IQ scores with SEM as probative evidence, so long as no numerical pattern is treated as dispositive and the court does not terminate the analysis at prong one. Chief Justice Roberts’s narrower rule best fits those precedents as written: reverse any framework that uses aggregation to screen out defendants when SEM-adjusted ranges keep 70 in play, while rejecting the Eleventh Circuit’s apparent move toward a one-way presumption untethered to Atkins’s implementation discretion and § 3596(c)’s text. The remedy, in my view, is to clarify the prohibition on conclusive score-counting—not to constitutionalize a rule that effectively compels prong-one satisfaction whenever any confidence interval touches 70.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts is right that Hall and Moore do not mandate a “one-low-score” rule and that factfinders may consider multiple IQ scores with SEM, but his proposed narrow reversal risks underspecifying the procedural-fairness problem: Alabama’s “mostly-above-70” aggregation can function as a de facto cutoff that makes SEM recognition nonoperative and effectively screens out prongs two and three. Justice Alito’s and Justice Kavanaugh’s worry about a defendant-favoring ratchet misframes what is constitutionally required; the floor is not a presumption from any single score, but a prohibition on using score-counting as dispositive when SEM-adjusted ranges keep 70 in play and the clinical record calls for a holistic Atkins inquiry. Justice Thomas’s federalism critique would require retreat from Hall/Moore’s insistence on clinically grounded reliability in applying a categorical Eighth Amendment exemption, and under stare decisis and the practical consequence of avoiding execution of an intellectually disabled person, I do not think we can bless a method that predictably recreates forbidden gatekeeping in operation. On this record, the constitutional defect is the mechanistic aggregation’s cutoff-like role, not the mere consideration of multiple scores.

John Roberts.reasoning: Atkins v. Virginia leaves States substantial discretion to develop procedures for identifying intellectual disability, and neither Hall v. Florida nor Moore v. Texas forbids courts from considering the full record of IQ testing so long as they do not impose a rigid cutoff that forecloses further inquiry. Hall requires accounting for the standard error of measurement and rejecting rules that treat 70 as an absolute bar, but it does not mandate that any one score within the SEM compels an Atkins finding when multiple other scores and other evidence point the other way. A cumulative-evidence approach that evaluates repeated scores (with SEM) alongside adaptive-functioning and onset evidence is consistent with Eighth Amendment doctrine and respects federalism while avoiding the categorical “no further exploration” rule Hall condemned. Because the Eleventh Circuit’s approach appears to constrain that permissible evidentiary weighing and risks converting SEM recognition into a one-way ratchet, I would reverse.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Atkins v. Virginia held only that the Eighth Amendment bars executing the intellectually disabled, while expressly leaving to the States “the task of developing appropriate ways to enforce” that restriction; nothing in the Constitution’s text or original public meaning requires any particular evidentiary method for weighing IQ scores. Hall v. Florida and Moore v. Texas improperly constitutionalize evolving clinical standards (including SEM and particular score-treatment rules) and thereby displace state authority in an area Atkins reserved to the States, so I would not extend those decisions to forbid Alabama from considering the cumulative evidentiary weight of multiple test scores. Under the Federal Death Penalty Act’s parallel bar, 18 U.S.C. § 3596(c), the question remains one of proof of “intellectual disability,” and it is reasonable for a court to treat a consistent pattern of scores above 70 as probative on the “significantly subaverage intellectual functioning” element rather than making any single score dispositive. Accordingly, I would reverse the Eleventh Circuit’s approach to the extent it constrains the State’s evidentiary framework beyond Atkins’s narrow categorical holding.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Atkins left it “to the States” to develop appropriate procedures for identifying intellectual disability in capital cases, and nothing in the Eighth Amendment or the FDPA’s parallel bar, 18 U.S.C. § 3596(c), requires a one-low-score rule or forbids courts from weighing the cumulative evidentiary force of multiple IQ results. Hall v. Florida prohibits rigid bright-line cutoffs that ignore the standard error of measurement, but it does not disable a factfinder from concluding—based on repeated testing clustered above 70—that the defendant has not carried the burden of proving “significantly subaverage intellectual functioning.” Moore likewise polices misuse of nonclinical factors, not the ordinary evidentiary practice of considering the full testing record and its practical implications for reliability. The Eleventh Circuit’s approach risks transforming Hall into a defendant-favoring presumption from any marginal score, undermining finality and States’ ability to enforce lawful capital sentences.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Atkins v. Virginia and the Federal Death Penalty Act, 18 U.S.C. § 3596(c), reflect a categorical constitutional and statutory bar on executing people with intellectual disability, and the Eighth Amendment requires procedures that reliably identify that class. Under Hall v. Florida, courts must account for the standard error of measurement and may not use IQ evidence in a way that functionally reinstates a rigid cutoff—whether by a single-score rule or by aggregating mostly-above-70 scores to treat 70 as dispositive. Moore v. Texas (2017) and Moore v. Texas (2019) further require alignment with current clinical standards and a holistic assessment of intellectual functioning and adaptive deficits, not score-counting that increases the risk of executing the intellectually disabled. Because Alabama’s cumulative-score approach risks elevating form over substance and denying protection to vulnerable defendants whose true functioning may fall within the SEM around 70, I would affirm that courts must consider multiple scores only in a manner consistent with Hall’s measurement-error framework and the full clinical picture.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Hall v. Florida forbids States from using an IQ score “above 70” as a conclusive bar to Atkins relief when 70 falls within the test’s standard error of measurement, and Moore v. Texas reinforces that the inquiry must be aligned with current clinical understanding rather than rigid score-counting rules. Multiple scores may of course be relevant evidence, but the Eighth Amendment does not permit aggregating mostly-above-70 scores into a de facto bright-line rule that forecloses considering SEM-adjusted ranges and the rest of the Atkins criteria, including adaptive functioning and developmental onset. A workable approach is to treat repeated testing as part of the totality of evidence—considering confidence intervals, practice effects, and test conditions—without converting the pattern into an automatic disqualification. That framework best fits Atkins’s categorical bar and avoids the constitutional error Hall identified while still allowing States meaningful factfinding under 18 U.S.C. § 3596(c)’s parallel prohibition.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Hall v. Florida forbids treating an IQ score above 70 as a conclusive gatekeeping bar when 70 falls within the score’s inherent standard error of measurement, and it requires courts to proceed to consider other evidence rather than end the inquiry at prong one. Allowing the State to aggregate multiple above-70 scores in a way that functionally re-creates a bright-line cutoff would evade Hall’s command and risk the unconstitutional execution of a person with intellectual disability under Atkins v. Virginia. Moore v. Texas further instructs that States may not employ methods that depart from prevailing clinical understandings so as to diminish the protection Atkins guarantees, and a mechanical “score-counting” approach does just that. Consistent with § 3596(c)’s parallel prohibition and the Eighth Amendment’s categorical bar, courts may consider multiple scores as evidence, but they must account for measurement error and cannot treat an above-70 pattern as dispositive in the face of SEM and other relevant proof.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Atkins v. Virginia left to the States (and, here, Congress via 18 U.S.C. § 3596(c)) primary responsibility to implement workable procedures for determining intellectual disability, subject to the Eighth Amendment. Hall v. Florida and Moore v. Texas forbid rigid score cutoffs and require courts to account for IQ-test measurement error and to avoid non-clinical distortions, but they do not mandate a one-low-score rule or bar courts from considering the full evidentiary picture created by multiple IQ scores. Given repeated scores above 70, a State may permissibly treat the pattern of testing results as probative of whether the defendant has shown “significantly subaverage intellectual functioning,” so long as the court still considers SEM/confidence intervals and the remaining Atkins prongs (adaptive deficits and onset before 18). The Eleventh Circuit’s approach unduly constrained that flexibility and, as a practical matter, risked converting Hall into a categorical rule contrary to the restrained, precedent-based framework of Atkins and its progeny.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Atkins leaves to the States (and, in the federal system, to Congress under 18 U.S.C. § 3596(c)) the task of implementing procedures to identify intellectual disability, and nothing in the Eighth Amendment’s text or this Court’s precedents forbids a factfinder from considering the full evidentiary record, including multiple IQ scores, when assessing “significantly subaverage intellectual functioning.” Hall v. Florida prohibits treating a single above-70 score as conclusively disqualifying when 70 falls within that score’s standard error of measurement, but it does not require courts to ignore a repeated pattern of scores above 70 or to treat SEM as a one-way ratchet. So long as Alabama’s framework does not reinstate a rigid cutoff (i.e., it permits consideration of SEM and other evidence, including adaptive functioning and onset), the Constitution allows a cumulative-evidence approach rather than a rule that any one qualifying score compels prong-one satisfaction. The Eleventh Circuit’s approach, as described, risks converting Hall’s anti-bright-line rule into a quasi-presumption for defendants and unduly constrains States’ permissible implementation choices under Atkins.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Atkins v. Virginia and the FDPA’s parallel bar, 18 U.S.C. § 3596(c), require a reliable, clinically grounded determination of intellectual disability, and Hall v. Florida forbids treating IQ evidence as “final and conclusive” through rigid numerical rules that ignore measurement error. When multiple IQ scores are presented, courts may consider them, but they must do so in a manner consistent with Hall and Moore v. Texas—i.e., accounting for the standard error of measurement and avoiding a cumulative “score-counting” approach that functionally reinstates a bright-line cutoff at 70. Given the Eighth Amendment’s demand for procedural fairness in a categorical exemption from execution, the inquiry must remain holistic, integrating IQ evidence (with confidence intervals) alongside adaptive functioning and onset before age 18. Alabama’s approach, as applied to treat a pattern of mostly above-70 scores as effectively dispositive against an Atkins claim, risks the same constitutional flaw Hall identified by elevating numerics over clinically informed judgment and practical reliability.

case_analysis.focal_point: Whether, in evaluating an Atkins intellectual-disability claim, courts may (or must) consider the cumulative pattern of multiple IQ scores—most of which exceed 70—in deciding if a defendant has shown significantly subaverage intellectual functioning that bars execution.
case_analysis.legal_provision: Eighth Amendment (as applied through Atkins v. Virginia’s categorical bar on executing intellectually disabled persons), with related federal statutory context from the Federal Death Penalty Act, 18 U.S.C. § 3596(c).
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Alabama argues that its evidentiary framework for proving intellectual disability is constitutionally permissible and consistent with this Court’s post-Atkins cases because it allows courts to assess all relevant evidence—including multiple IQ scores and their overall distribution—rather than treating any single score (or the lowest score) as dispositive. Given respondent’s series of scores (e.g., 75, 74, 72, 78, 74), petitioner contends he has not plausibly shown that his true IQ is 70 or below once proper psychometric principles are applied, and the Eleventh Circuit wrongly allowed the Atkins claim to proceed by misapplying this Court’s precedents and unduly restricting state experimentation in administering Atkins.
case_analysis.respondent_position: Smith argues that under Atkins and this Court’s subsequent decisions, states may not employ IQ-score rules or cumulative-score reasoning that functionally raises the eligibility threshold above what prevailing clinical standards permit, or that discount the standard error of measurement and related clinical considerations. He contends that courts must interpret IQ testing in a manner faithful to current medical/psychological practice—accounting for measurement error and avoiding rigid numerical cutoffs—so that individuals who are in fact intellectually disabled are not exposed to execution merely because several scores fall modestly above 70.

John Roberts.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor and Justice Kagan make the strongest point: a “cumulative pattern” of mostly-above-70 scores can, in practice, become a de facto cutoff that recreates the rigidity Hall condemned and short-circuits the “further exploration” Hall requires once a score falls within the SEM-adjusted range. But Hall and Moore prohibit treating any IQ arithmetic as “final and conclusive”; they do not constitutionalize a lowest-score-controls rule, and Atkins leaves States room to structure evidentiary weighing so long as it remains individualized, SEM-aware, and clinically informed. The constitutional defect arises only if Alabama’s approach functions as a presumption or categorical bar (as Justice Kagan worries), not from the mere consideration of multiple scores alongside adaptive functioning and onset. Nothing in § 3596(c) supplies a different constitutional rule; it announces the substantive bar but does not mandate a particular method of weighing IQ evidence beyond what Hall/Moore already require.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s and Justice Kagan’s strongest point is the practical risk that Alabama’s “cumulative pattern” could harden into a de facto >70 cutoff and thereby replicate Hall’s condemned rigidity. But as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Alito explain, Hall and Moore prohibit treating any IQ score or arithmetic method as “final and conclusive” and require SEM-aware, clinically informed consideration; they do not constitutionalize a lowest-score-controls rule or disable a factfinder from weighing the full testing record alongside adaptive functioning and onset. Under an original public meaning approach to the Eighth Amendment—and consistent with Atkins’ express deference to state implementation—we have no warrant to impose a federal tie-breaker absent a showing that Alabama’s rule, on its face or in operation, forecloses SEM-adjusted inquiry and the “further exploration” Hall requires. The respondents’ concerns go to potential as-applied misuse; they do not justify converting contested psychometric weighting into a constitutional command.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor and Justice Kagan raise the most serious concern: that a “cumulative pattern” of mostly-above-70 scores could function as a de facto cutoff, recreating the rigidity Hall condemned. But that is an as-applied risk, not a basis for converting Hall and Moore into a constitutional command that the lowest score within the SEM must control, which would itself harden into an inflexible tie-breaker untethered to the Eighth Amendment’s text and Atkins’ allocation of implementation discretion to the States. Chief Justice Roberts’s framing is persuasive that the constitutional fault line is whether the State treats IQ arithmetic as “final and conclusive” or uses aggregation as an operative presumption that forecloses SEM-triggered “further exploration,” not whether the factfinder may consider the full testing record alongside adaptive functioning and onset. Unless Alabama’s approach is shown to operate as a categorical bar in practice, I see no warrant to constitutionalize respondent’s preferred evidentiary weighting rule.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts’s narrowing proposal usefully clarifies that Hall and Moore do not constitutionalize a “lowest-score-controls” rule and that a State may consider the full testing record, but it does not cure the practical Eighth Amendment risk if Alabama’s “cumulative pattern” operates as a functional presumption that modestly >70 scores defeat the claim. Justice Alito and Justice Kavanaugh frame this as ordinary evidentiary weighing, yet Hall’s central command is that when an IQ score falls within the SEM-adjusted range implicating 70, the Constitution requires “further exploration” rather than a heuristic that predictably dilutes SEM and systematically under-identifies disability. Moore reinforces that point by forbidding state-devised approaches untethered from contemporary clinical understanding that narrow Atkins’ protected class in operation, even if not in form. Under my pragmatic, fairness-focused approach, the dispositive question is real-world error risk—here, that aggregation becomes a backdoor elevated cutoff—so I remain with Respondent.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts’s narrowing proposal is the strongest petitioner argument: Hall and Moore do not compel a lowest-score-controls rule, and a State may consider the full testing record so long as nothing is treated as “final and conclusive.” But the constitutional problem here is functional, not formal—Alabama’s “cumulative pattern” risks becoming a de facto presumption that a run of modestly >70 scores defeats the claim, which effectively dilutes SEM and short-circuits Hall’s required “further exploration” once any score implicates the 70 range. Justice Alito’s insistence that this is merely an as-applied evidentiary question understates Moore’s constraint: a state-devised heuristic untethered to accepted clinical practice that predictably under-identifies disability is itself the Eighth Amendment problem, even if it is described as “holistic.” Pragmatically and textually, I can accept multiple-score consideration, but not a method that elevates the operative threshold above what psychometrics support and thereby recreates Hall’s rigidity under a different label.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor and Justice Kagan offer the strongest objection: that Alabama’s “cumulative pattern” may operate as a functional >70 cutoff that recreates Hall’s forbidden rigidity by diluting SEM-triggered “further exploration.” But as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Thomas emphasize, Hall and Moore prohibit making an IQ number (or any arithmetic with IQ numbers) “final and conclusive” and require a clinically informed, SEM-aware, individualized inquiry; they do not constitutionalize respondent’s competing rigidity—a lowest-score-controls rule—and Atkins leaves implementation space to the States absent a rule that forecloses consideration of SEM-adjusted low scores and adaptive-functioning evidence. The constitutional line, in my view, is crossed only if Alabama’s aggregation operates as an operative presumption or categorical bar that shuts down SEM-informed exploration, which sounds in an as-applied defect rather than a freestanding federal mandate about how to weigh multiple scores. Separation-of-powers principles counsel against converting contested psychometric tie-breakers into Eighth Amendment doctrine without a demonstrated state rule (express or de facto) that systematically prevents consideration of qualifying evidence.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor and Justice Kagan’s strongest point is practical and serious: a “cumulative pattern” of mostly-above-70 scores can, in application, harden into a functional cutoff that dilutes SEM and risks evading Hall’s command for “further exploration.” But I agree with Chief Justice Roberts that Hall and Moore are best read as anti-rigidity precedents: they bar treating any IQ arithmetic as “final and conclusive” and require SEM-sensitive, clinically informed consideration plus adaptive-functioning and onset evidence, not a constitutionalized lowest-score-controls rule. The constitutional problem arises only if Alabama’s approach operates as an actual presumption that forecloses inquiry once there are enough >70 scores; absent that kind of dispositive rule, Atkins leaves states room to weigh the full testing record within an individualized assessment. I therefore stay with Petitioner, while emphasizing (as Roberts does) that any express or de facto elevation of the operative threshold above what SEM-aware practice permits would cross the Hall/Moore line.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s and Justice Kagan’s strongest point is that a “cumulative pattern” of >70 scores can become a functional presumption that dilutes SEM and recreates Hall’s condemned rigidity; that risk is real and must be policed. But I agree with Chief Justice Roberts that Hall and Moore draw the constitutional line at rules (or their functional equivalents) that make an IQ number “final and conclusive” or that foreclose SEM-sensitive “further exploration” and adaptive-functioning evidence—not at a State’s allowing the factfinder, consistent with clinical practice, to consider the full testing record. On an originalist/textualist reading of the Eighth Amendment as implemented through Atkins’ state-deference framework, the Constitution does not mandate a lowest-score-dispositive tie-breaker; it requires only an individualized, clinically informed inquiry in which aggregation cannot operate as an automatic bar. Absent a showing that Alabama’s method actually functions as a categorical cutoff in practice, I would adhere to the petitioner-side narrow rule and leave as-applied challenges available.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts’s narrow formulation is the strongest petitioner-side answer because it correctly rejects any constitutional “lowest-score-controls” rule and preserves room to weigh the full testing record. But that framing, echoed by Justice Thomas’s Atkins deference point, still leaves unresolved the practical/procedural question Hall and Moore force us to ask: whether Alabama’s “cumulative pattern” functions as a de facto elevated cutoff by treating a cluster of modestly >70 scores as effectively dispositive and thereby short-circuiting SEM-triggered “further exploration.” Under Moore’s command that state methodologies be clinically informed rather than state-devised heuristics that systematically narrow the protected class, aggregation cannot be allowed to dilute SEM into irrelevance or substitute for individualized inquiry into adaptive deficits and onset. Because the risk here is not abstract but structural—creating an unacceptable likelihood of executing someone categorically exempt—I would hold the method unconstitutional to the extent it operates as a functional presumption against disability once several scores exceed 70.

John Roberts.reasoning: Atkins left the States with substantial discretion to develop procedures for identifying intellectual disability, and Hall and Moore principally forbid rigid rules that treat a single IQ score (or a fixed 70 cutoff) as dispositive while disregarding the standard error of measurement and adaptive-function evidence. Nothing in Hall requires a court to ignore the full record of testing; to the contrary, it criticized schemes that make an IQ number “final and conclusive” and emphasized consideration of “other evidence,” which is consistent with evaluating multiple scores along with clinical principles. A narrow ruling respecting federalism and precedent would hold that the Eighth Amendment permits (but does not mandate) consideration of the cumulative pattern of IQ scores so long as the State’s approach does not operate as a de facto bright-line threshold above 70 and remains tethered to accepted psychometric practice. That disposition preserves institutional legitimacy by enforcing Hall/Moore’s anti-rigidity principle without constitutionalizing a one-score-or-lowest-score rule.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The Eighth Amendment, as originally understood, does not constitutionalize evolving clinical standards for diagnosing intellectual disability, and Atkins v. Virginia expressly left to the States “the task of developing appropriate ways to enforce” its bar. Alabama’s approach—considering all relevant evidence, including multiple IQ scores and their overall pattern—fits within that discretion and does not impose the kind of rigid cutoff rule invalidated in Hall v. Florida. Hall and Moore v. Texas should not be read to require courts to privilege a single low score or to adopt medical organizations’ views as constitutional commands; they at most prevent States from using bright-line rules that foreclose consideration of SEM and other evidence. Given respondent’s series of scores mostly above 70, Alabama may evaluate the cumulative record to determine whether he has carried his burden to show “significantly subaverage intellectual functioning” under Atkins and consistent with 18 U.S.C. § 3596(c)’s general bar on executing the intellectually disabled.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Atkins v. Virginia leaves to the States the primary responsibility for developing workable procedures to identify intellectual disability, and neither the Eighth Amendment nor 18 U.S.C. § 3596(c) compels a one-low-score rule that treats a marginal IQ result as dispositive. Hall v. Florida forbids a rigid cutoff that prevents any consideration of the standard error of measurement and related evidence, but it does not bar courts from considering multiple IQ scores cumulatively, so long as SEM is respected and the inquiry remains clinically informed. Moore v. Texas likewise requires courts to use current medical guidance and avoid idiosyncratic distortions, not to ignore the practical evidentiary significance of a consistent pattern of scores mostly above 70. Alabama’s approach—assessing all relevant evidence, including the distribution of scores and psychometric principles—fits within the discretion Hall and Moore acknowledge and better serves the practical need for reliable determinations in capital cases.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Under Atkins v. Virginia the Eighth Amendment categorically bars executing people with intellectual disability, and Hall v. Florida requires courts to account for the standard error of measurement and forbids rigid (or de facto) numerical cutoffs that create an unacceptable risk of executing an intellectually disabled person. A “cumulative pattern” approach that treats several scores modestly above 70 as effectively dispositive can operate like the kind of cutoff Hall rejected, especially if it discounts measurement error and other clinically relevant factors. Moore v. Texas (2017) and Moore v. Texas (2019) further require that adjudication be guided by current medical standards rather than state-created heuristics that narrow Atkins’ protection. Alabama may consider multiple IQ scores as part of a holistic inquiry, but it may not use their distribution to raise the functional threshold above what clinical practice recognizes and thereby expose vulnerable defendants to execution in violation of the Eighth Amendment (and consistent with 18 U.S.C. § 3596(c)’s bar on executing the intellectually disabled).

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Hall v. Florida forbids States from using IQ evidence in a manner that functions as a rigid cutoff at 70 by refusing to account for the standard error of measurement (SEM) and thereby foreclosing meaningful consideration of intellectual disability. Allowing courts to treat a “cumulative pattern” of multiple scores—most modestly above 70—as effectively dispositive risks recreating the very rigidity Hall rejected, especially where one or more scores fall within the SEM-adjusted range implicating 70 or below and thus require “further exploration.” Moore v. Texas (2017, 2019) reinforces that Atkins determinations must be informed by current clinical standards and cannot employ methodologies that systematically under-identify intellectual disability. Consistent with the Eighth Amendment rule of Atkins and the FDPA’s parallel bar in 18 U.S.C. § 3596(c), courts may consider all relevant evidence, but they may not use multiple-score aggregation as a workaround that elevates the constitutional threshold above what psychometric principles permit.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Atkins v. Virginia left to the States (and Congress) the task of implementing procedures to identify intellectual disability, and neither the Eighth Amendment’s text nor 18 U.S.C. § 3596(c) prescribes an IQ-only, lowest-score-controls rule. Hall v. Florida and Moore v. Texas forbid rigid numerical cutoffs and require attention to the standard error of measurement and adaptive functioning, but they do not prevent a court from considering the full body of relevant evidence, including the cumulative pattern and reliability of multiple IQ scores, to decide whether the defendant has carried his burden. Allowing a factfinder to weigh several scores—most above 70—does not recreate Florida’s conclusive 70-point rule; it reflects ordinary evidentiary reasoning and preserves the separation-of-powers deference Atkins contemplated to state procedural choices. Where the evidence is mixed and the claim turns on borderline psychometrics, the Constitution demands individualized, clinically informed consideration, not a mandated dispositive inference from a single low score.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Atkins v. Virginia established a categorical Eighth Amendment bar but left States substantial discretion to develop workable procedures for adjudicating intellectual-disability claims, and neither Hall v. Florida nor Moore v. Texas imposed a one-low-score rule that makes any single borderline IQ score dispositive. Hall forbids rigid cutoffs and requires accounting for the standard error of measurement, but it also contemplates individualized evaluation consistent with clinical practice, which ordinarily considers the full testing record rather than ignoring multiple scores above 70. Given that respondent’s testing history reflects several scores above 70, Alabama may consider the cumulative pattern of scores—so long as it properly accounts for measurement error and does not create a de facto higher cutoff—in determining whether “significantly subaverage intellectual functioning” is proved under Atkins (and consistent with the FDPA’s bar, 18 U.S.C. § 3596(c)). The Eleventh Circuit’s approach risks displacing state experimentation and undermining administrable standards by effectively treating the lowest score as controlling.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Atkins v. Virginia left to the States the task of developing “appropriate ways” to enforce the Eighth Amendment’s bar, subject to this Court’s limits in Hall and Moore that States may not adopt rigid rules that treat an IQ number as dispositive or disregard the standard error of measurement. Considering the full pattern of multiple IQ scores—including that most exceed 70—does not itself impose an unconstitutional bright-line cutoff; it is instead an evidentiary assessment consistent with Hall’s instruction to avoid treating any single score as “final and conclusive” and to evaluate intellectual functioning in light of all relevant evidence. So long as Alabama’s approach permits the defendant to rely on the SEM and present adaptive-functioning and developmental-onset evidence, it falls within the permissible discretion Atkins contemplated and does not “raise the threshold” by rule rather than by proof. Nothing in 18 U.S.C. § 3596(c) requires treating the lowest IQ score as controlling; it bars execution of the intellectually disabled, leaving courts to evaluate the evidence under constitutionally valid standards.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Under Atkins v. Virginia and the Eighth Amendment, a State’s procedures must reliably identify individuals with intellectual disability and may not create a heightened, functional cutoff that risks executing those categorically protected. Hall v. Florida rejects treating any numerical threshold (including through methods that effectively privilege higher scores) as “final and conclusive,” and requires courts to account for the standard error of measurement and to consider adaptive-functioning and other clinical evidence rather than letting IQ arithmetic drive the result. Moore v. Texas further instructs that adjudications must be informed by current clinical standards and cannot use evidentiary heuristics that systematically discount disability. Accordingly, Alabama may consider multiple IQ scores, but it may not rely on their cumulative pattern in a way that substitutes for clinically grounded, holistic factfinding and increases the risk of an unconstitutional execution.
